strengths: Addresses an important problem: missing sensitive attributes can distort fairness assessments. Training against adversarially challenging imputations is a useful direction for fair graph learning.

Several reported improvements are substantial. On BAIL, BFtS improves F1 from FairGNN’s 0.86 to 0.91 and reduces the equality-of-opportunity gap from 4.1% to 1.7%. GERMAN also shows meaningful fairness improvements.

The evaluation includes four real datasets, synthetic graphs with varying assortativity, GCN and GAT backbones, relevant FairGNN and RNF comparisons, and averages over ten runs. The appendix provides sensitivity analyses, partial ablations, pseudocode, and a code link.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees do not cover the actual training objective. Proposition 1 analyzes the adversarial-only game in Eq. 7, omitting the classification and imputation losses used in Eqs. 4 and 6. Minimizing classification loss plus a finite fairness penalty need not yield zero Jensen–Shannon divergence, so Theorem 1 does not establish demographic parity for the trained model. Replacing optimization over the imputation GNN with a supremum over imputations also requires explicit expressivity and admissibility assumptions.

The convergence argument contains substantive mathematical errors. Section 5.3 states that disjoint distributions have zero Jensen–Shannon divergence; their divergence is maximal. When imputation assigns everyone the same sensitive value, one conditional distribution is undefined. Furthermore, Corollary 1’s comparison of divergence values does not establish useful gradients or improved convergence of alternating neural-network training. The claimed convergence advantage is therefore unsupported.

There is an unresolved numerical inconsistency in the evaluation: Figure 3(a) plots an RNF value of approximately −2 for 1−ΔDP, although this quantity must lie in [0,1] under Eq. 9. This requires checking the metric computation or plotting pipeline. Table 1’s caption also overstates NBA accuracy dominance: BFtS has F1 0.70 versus vanilla’s 0.73.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of adversarial imputation. BFtS also introduces LDAM, which the paper explicitly credits for accuracy gains. Table 3 varies LDAM placement but does not provide a controlled β=0 ablation or LDAM-matched FairGNN comparison. Direct measurements showing that the learned imputations expose greater hidden bias are also missing; the kernel-PCA visualization does not establish this mechanism.

The missingness evaluation does not adequately test the motivating collection-bias scenario. The manuscript does not specify how observed sensitive attributes are selected. Varying their observed fraction alone does not establish robustness to missingness that depends on protected group, outcome, or graph position.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Eq. 3 conditions on binary imputed attributes without explaining how gradients reach the imputation network through those assignments. Eq. 2 mixes imputation and classification logits, and Figure 2’s caption contradicts the optimization directions in Eqs. 4–5. Exact validation/test splits, optimizer settings, and selected hyperparameters are also insufficiently documented. These issues limit reproducibility despite the repository link.
